locflow.hero.title: LocFlow — localization, your way.
locflow.hero.subtext: A pipeline that handles extraction, formatting, delivery and re-import — and plugs in AI translation, your own LLM, or a human vendor at whichever stage makes sense for your project.
locflow.features.title: What it does
locflow.features.lead: LocFlow manages the full localization lifecycle, scaled to your business needs.
locflow.features.li1: Extract strings from source files (JSON, PO, XLIFF, and custom formats)
locflow.features.li2: Format and package content for vendor delivery or automated processing
locflow.features.li3: Optional AI translation via GPT, Claude, or a custom LLM of your choice
locflow.features.li4: QA checks and glossary enforcement at any stage of the pipeline
locflow.features.li5: Re-import translated content back into your source system
locflow.features.li6: Configurable per project: fully automated, AI-assisted, or human-only
locflow.process.title: How it works
locflow.process.step1.title: Extract & format
locflow.process.step1.desc: The system tracks changes in the source language files. Source content is then parsed, cleaned and packaged into the target format for your workflow.
locflow.process.step2.title: Route & translate
locflow.process.step2.desc: Content is routed to an AI model, an external vendor, or both — based on your project configuration.
locflow.process.step3.title: Deliver & re-import
locflow.process.step3.desc: Translated files are delivered in the correct format and re-imported into the source system.
locflow.stack.title: Built to be swappable
locflow.stack.desc: Python, javascript and N8N-based pipeline with LLM support. The model layer is configurable — point it at your own LLM endpoint or bypass AI entirely and route straight to your translation vendor. No lock-in at any stage.
locflow.cta.title: Need a localization pipeline that fits how your team works?
locflow.cta.desc: LocFlow is in active development. Implementation is customized based on every project's unique requirements. If you're interested in an early version or a custom setup, let's talk.

lab.meta.title: Lab — Bad Idea Interactive
lab.intro.title: Lab
lab.intro.p1: Public R&D. Between client projects I build things to answer questions I can't answer by reading about them — how a mechanic feels, whether a pipeline holds, what breaks when real users show up.
lab.intro.p2: Some of it shipped. Some is still moving. Some is here because it didn't work, and that turned out to be the useful part.
lab.shipped.title: Shipped
lab.indevelopment.title: In development
lab.experiments.title: Experiments
lab.shelved.title: Shelved
lab.closing.text: This is how I work: scope it small, ship it, find out what the assumption got wrong. It's the same approach I bring into studios.
lab.shipped.mayor.title: Mayor Saves Christmas
lab.shipped.mayor.hook: An arcade platformer set in Vigo. Trap enemies, chain combos, save the city's Christmas lights.
lab.shipped.mayor.question: Could a small game be tied to a real-world event — Vigo's lights actually switching on — and would that synchronization earn anything a normal release wouldn't?
lab.shipped.mayor.findings: The real lesson was structural. I built and tested one solid gameplay loop first, then added worlds one at a time, each layered on without breaking what came before. Because the scope stayed small and every layer was additive, the game was releasable at any point — so the fixed real-world deadline stopped being a risk. Tying the launch to the actual event gave it a window and a reason for local players to care, but that only worked because the build was never in a half-finished state waiting on the next feature.
lab.shipped.escape.title: Escape From Hell
lab.shipped.escape.hook: A score-chasing arena runner about tight movement and one-more-run pressure.
lab.shipped.escape.question: What's the real distance between a prototype that feels good on my machine and something that ships to a store?
lab.shipped.escape.findings: Most of it was performance on mid-range Android and the Play Console work nobody warns you about — store submission is a project of its own, not a final step. Playtesting was the other half: it validated the core idea early, then did the work I couldn't do alone on UX and balance. I'd budget for both from the start now rather than discovering them at the end.
lab.indevelopment.mandarin.title: Mandarin Daily
lab.indevelopment.mandarin.hook: A flashcard app for Mandarin learners — HSK vocabulary, example sentences, spaced repetition, short daily sessions.
lab.indevelopment.mandarin.question: Spaced repetition tools optimise for retention and ignore whether anyone opens them on day nine. Can progression and customization do the work motivation usually has to?
lab.indevelopment.mandarin.findings: Progression matters more than the algorithm, and letting learners shape their own path matters nearly as much. Accessibility turned out to be structural rather than a nice-to-have — pinyin toggles, traditional and simplified — because without it whole groups of learners simply can't use the thing. The AI features (scanning documents into your own flashcards, reviewing homework) work, but the real lesson was cost: a feature that's cheap in testing is a different product at scale, and optimising for that changed what was worth building at all.
lab.indevelopment.coil.title: Coil
lab.indevelopment.coil.hook: A tracker for reptile keepers — collections, feeding schedules, shedding, health records.
lab.indevelopment.coil.question: Keepers already track this in notebooks and spreadsheets. Does an app actually beat the notebook, or just move the problem?
lab.indevelopment.coil.findings: Building against an existing need is far easier than manufacturing one — but only if you check the design against how people actually record things, not how you'd organise it yourself. Current work is accounts and cross-platform sync, since a collection that lives on one phone is a notebook with extra steps.
lab.experiments.bullethell.title: [Name pending] — bullet-hell prototype
lab.experiments.bullethell.hook: A pure prototype, deliberately unscoped beyond the core.
lab.experiments.bullethell.question: How much of a game's systems can I hand to AI before the design stops being mine? Implementation is AI-assisted; every big-picture design decision stays with me. Where that line actually falls is the experiment.
lab.experiments.bullethell.findings: [TO WRITE — in progress. Even a partial answer is worth having. Most current-feeling entry on the page and the one a consulting reader is most likely to stop on.]
lab.shelved.noescape.title: There Is No Escape
lab.shelved.noescape.hook: A grid-based game built in the world of Escape From Hell.
lab.shelved.noescape.question: Could an existing prototype's world carry a completely different genre, and does reusing your own IP actually save anything?
lab.shelved.noescape.findings:
Why it stopped: The core was fun, but growing it meant going well past the scope I'd set — and that expansion served neither a learning goal nor a market one. Fun on its own wasn't a good enough reason to keep going.

What it taught me: Time-boxing this kind of project is the whole discipline, and the basics have to be fun before anything gets built on top of them. Also that "I'm enjoying this" and "this is worth continuing" are different questions, and it's worth asking the second one out loud.
